entities.description: The winter solstice — the same real astronomical moment as the Yule sabbat (tropical Sun longitude 270°), reckoned here by direct solar-longitude search rather than by resolving a native lunisolar day, since the Chinese calendar's own month 11 is itself defined as "the month containing the winter solstice." In Taoist internal-alchemy (neidan) practice, Dongzhi marks the point of maximum yin from which yang begins its return — precisely the reading given to I Ching Hexagram 24 (Fu, "Return"), whose own text names the winter solstice directly ("the ancient kings closed the passes at the winter solstice"). This is a textually explicit correspondence, not an inferred one.

5th day of the 5th lunar month. Folk tradition holds that the Five Poisons (Wu Du) — typically the snake, scorpion, centipede, toad, and spider, though the exact set of five varies by region and era — reach their full seasonal potency at noon on this day, as summer heat brings out venomous and disease-bearing creatures. The response is apotropaic rather than avoidant: images of all five poisons, worn as amulets or embroidered onto children's clothing, are believed to accumulate enough poison of their own to counteract the pernicious influences they represent — fighting poison with poison. Other period customs include drinking realgar wine, hanging mugwort and calamus at doorways, and displaying charms of Zhong Kui, the demon-queller.
